# Evolution {#sec-evolution}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
How does evolution affect the current genomes? Gene duplication,
evolutionary pressure.
:::

## Introduction

Dobzhansky's remark that "nothing in biology makes sense except in the
light of evolution" is particularly true for bioinformatics. Almost every method that
transfers information from one sequence to another assumes common
descent. The genomes we see today are shaped by mutation, which creates
variation, and by natural selection and genetic drift, which determine
whether variants are lost or become fixed. The neutral theory
[@kimura1968] proposed that most changes fixed at the molecular level are
selectively neutral and become fixed by drift. This explains the roughly
clock-like accumulation of substitutions that makes it possible to date
divergences [@zuckerkandl1963; @langley1974]. Selection can be detected by
comparing the rate of non-synonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS):
values much below one indicate purifying selection, and values above one
indicate positive selection [@yang2000].

Homologous genes fall into different classes depending on the event that
separated them [@fitch1970; @koonin2005]. *Orthologs* diverged by
speciation, *paralogs* by gene duplication, and *xenologs* by horizontal
gene transfer. The distinction matters because orthologs are generally
expected to keep the same function, while paralogs are free to diverge.
Orthology can be inferred from graphs of reciprocal best hits, as in COG
and InParanoid [@tatusov1997; @remm2001], or from gene trees reconciled
with the species tree, as in OrthoFinder [@goodman1979; @emms2019]. Each
approach has its own strengths and failure modes [@altenhoff2019].

Gene duplication is the main source of new genes. Most duplicates are
lost, but some are kept because they split the ancestral functions
between them (subfunctionalisation) or acquire new ones
(neofunctionalisation) [@ohno1968; @lynch2000]. Whole-genome duplications
have occurred repeatedly, for example twice early in vertebrate evolution
and several times in plants. In proteins, evolution also works at the
level of domains. New architectures arise when existing domains are
duplicated, fused, split or shuffled
[@apic2001; @bjorklund2005; @levy2008]. In prokaryotes, horizontal gene
transfer is a major force, and it, rather than duplication, drives the
expansion of most protein families [@treangen2011].

Population genetics also helps explain why genomes differ in structure.
Lynch argued that the small effective population sizes of multicellular
eukaryotes weaken selection against slightly harmful additions, such as
introns and mobile elements. Genomic complexity can therefore build up
without being adaptive [@lynch2003]. This view connects evolution with
@sec-genomes. Evolutionary relationships are reconstructed with the
methods described in @sec-phylogeny.

## Key concepts

- Mutation, selection, genetic drift, effective population size; genetic hitchhiking
- Neutral theory and the molecular clock
- Homology, orthology, paralogy (in- and out-paralogs), xenology; analogy/convergence
- Orthology inference: reciprocal best hits, COGs, InParanoid, OrthoFinder; tree-based vs. graph-based methods
- Gene duplication and its fates (non-/sub-/neofunctionalisation); whole-genome duplication (Ohno's 2R hypothesis)
- Detecting selection: dN/dS (Ka/Ks), site and branch models
- Protein domain evolution: domain combinations, gene fusion and fission
- Horizontal gene transfer and its role in prokaryotes
- Gene trees vs. species trees, reconciliation

## Key papers

::: {.callout-tip}
★ = mandatory in earlier reading lists.
:::

### Reviews — start here

- ★ @altenhoff2019 — inferring orthology and paralogy.
- @koonin2005 — orthologs, paralogs and evolutionary genomics.
- @koonin2011 — are there laws of genome evolution?
- @doolittle2010 — the roots of bioinformatics in protein evolution.

### Classic papers

- @zuckerkandl1963 — chemical paleogenetics: ancestral reconstruction.
- @kimura1968 — evolutionary rate at the molecular level (neutral theory).
- @ohno1968 — evolution by gene duplication.
- @fitch1970 — distinguishing homologous from analogous proteins (orthology/paralogy defined).
- @langley1974 — constancy of the rate of molecular evolution.
- @goodman1979 — reconciling gene trees with species trees.
- @fitch2000 — homology: a personal view.

### Gene duplication and genome complexity

- @lynch2000 — the evolutionary fate and consequences of duplicate genes.
- @lynch2003 — the origins of genome complexity.

### Orthology and comparative genomics

- @tatusov1997 — clusters of orthologous groups (COGs).
- @remm2001 — InParanoid: orthologs and in-paralogs.
- @emms2019 — OrthoFinder.

### Domains and protein evolution

- @apic2001 — domain combinations in the three domains of life.
- @bjorklund2005 — domain rearrangements in protein evolution.
- @levy2008 — assembly of protein complexes reflects evolution.

### Selection and horizontal transfer

- @yang2000 — statistical methods for detecting molecular adaptation.
- @treangen2011 — horizontal transfer, not duplication, drives gene family expansion in prokaryotes.
